items.title: Half-life is a probability, not a clock
items.claim: A radioactive nucleus has a half-life of 5730 years. People imagine each atom has a 5730-year fuse. In fact each atom's decay is fundamentally random — no ageing, no internal clock.
items.prompt: If you watch a single carbon-14 nucleus for 5730 years, what is the chance it decays in the next year?

options.text: Almost 100 percent — it's used up its half-life
About 1 in 8267 — exactly the same as a freshly made C-14 nucleus

items.reveal:
The probability of decay per unit time (decay constant lambda) is fixed for a given isotope. A nucleus 'remembers' nothing about how long it has existed. For C-14, lambda equals ln 2 over 5730 years, so per year the decay chance is about 1 part in 8267 — for every individual nucleus, every year.

Half-life emerges from large populations of identical-but-independent random events. With one nucleus there is no half-life — only a probability distribution. With Avogadro's number of nuclei the law of large numbers makes the exponential decay law deterministic.

This is fundamentally different from human ageing or battery discharge — those have internal state that changes with time.
items.why: Half-life is intuitively pictured as countdown. It's actually a statistical property of populations of memoryless processes.

items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Oxygen exists as a molecule with TWO unpaired electrons
items.claim: O2 is a closed-shell, even-electron molecule. By the textbook Lewis structure (O=O), all electrons are paired. Yet liquid oxygen is magnetic — drip it between the poles of a strong magnet and it sticks.

options.text: Liquid O2 contains impurities of iron
Molecular orbital theory shows O2's highest occupied orbitals are two degenerate pi-antibonding orbitals, each holding ONE electron — by Hund's rule, both are unpaired
Liquid O2 is actually O3 in disguise
Magnetic fields ionise O2 into charged species

items.reveal_title: Lewis dot structures don't capture orbital occupancy
items.reveal:
Build O2's MO diagram: combine atomic orbitals of two oxygens. Filling 16 electrons in order gives a configuration ending with (pi*) squared — but the two pi-antibonding orbitals are degenerate, and by Hund's rule each gets one electron with parallel spins.

The molecule has bond order 2 (matches O=O) but it also has 2 unpaired electrons (does not match O=O). Lewis structures are a useful shorthand but they hide quantum mechanical detail.

Videos of liquid oxygen being held in place between magnet poles are striking — the same thing that lets O2 carry around our blood is the same thing that holds it to a magnet.
items.why: Lewis structures count electrons in pairs and tell you nothing about magnetism. Molecular orbital theory does — and is correct.
